fable-5.1.text:
When we started SSI, the idea was that we would be a research-only company. We would go straight to superintelligence, and we wouldn't be distracted by the rat race of releasing products every few months. And I still think there's a lot of merit to that. The rat race is a real thing. It makes it harder to do the kind of research that actually requires you to go away and think for a while.

But I've been changing my mind on this, at least partially, and the reason is the following. If you ask what is actually going to make AI safe, I think the answer is not primarily that one lab has figured out the right technique in secret. I think it has a lot to do with the world seeing what the AI can do. When people see the capability, they respond. Governments respond, other labs respond, the public responds. And the reaction is, in my opinion, quite a bit more sensible than it would have been if the capability had just appeared all at once.

So there's this argument that incremental exposure is a safety mechanism in itself. If the AI is powerful and people can see that it's powerful, then the behavior of everyone, including the companies building it, is going to change. Nobody wants to be the one who messes up when everyone is watching. That pressure is quite valuable, and you don't get it if you're sitting in a building somewhere doing research that nobody can see.

There's a second thing, which is more about us specifically. If you want to have an effect on how this goes, if you want to be able to say, "here is how we think it should be done, here is what safe looks like," it is much easier to do that when you have something people can look at. When you have a model that people use, people take you seriously in a different way. If you only have ideas, that's harder.

So I'm not saying we've concluded that we need to release a product. I'm saying that the original argument, that it's cleaner to just go straight for it, has a real cost that I underappreciated. Whether the right answer is to release something ourselves, or to find some other way to be part of that public process, that is something we are still thinking about. But the case for being completely out of the public eye is weaker than I thought it was a year or two ago.

r001.rationale: The response says that people seeing AI capabilities prompts reactions and can improve safety, but it does not compare that experience with reading an essay predicting AI’s capabilities.

opus-5.5.text:
I think the core issue is that it's very hard to imagine. When people talk about AI, about AGI, about superintelligence, they're talking about something that doesn't exist yet. You can write essays and make arguments, but you can't really feel it. I've noticed this with myself, too. You look at the systems we have today, and they make mistakes, they do strange things, and it's hard to internalize that the future will be genuinely different.

So the original idea with SSI was the straight shot. You don't participate in the market race, you don't make all the compromises that come with having a product, and you focus on the research and on getting it right. There's real merit to that. But I've come to put more weight on the value of the world actually seeing the AI. Gradual release, people interacting with the systems, feeling their power and also their weaknesses. That's what changes behavior.

And I think behavior will change a lot. As the AI becomes visibly more powerful, I expect companies, including fierce competitors, to start collaborating on safety in ways they don't today. You already see the early signs. I expect governments and the public to want to do something. That only happens if people see it. If you build it quietly in a lab and then present something very powerful all at once, you deny the world the chance to adjust, to build intuition, and to push back where it needs to. So exposure isn't only a commercial question. It's part of how the whole thing goes well. That's why the straight-shot plan deserves another look, even if the research focus stays the same.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts essays and arguments, which people cannot really feel, with gradual release and direct interaction that lets people experience AI’s power and weaknesses and changes behavior.

fable-5.text:
So the reasoning goes something like this. The original logic of the straight shot was: you insulate yourself from the market, from the rat race, and you just work on the safe superintelligence directly, and you don't get distracted by products, you don't get pulled into the competitive dynamics. And that logic is real, it has merit.

But there is a consideration that pushes in the other direction, and I think it's an important one, which is that it's actually very valuable for the world to see the AI. When people only hear about AI as a concept, as an abstraction, it doesn't really register. But when the AI is out there and people interact with it and they feel what it can do, then everyone — the public, governments, institutions — they start to respond. They start to adapt, they start to care about safety, they start to prepare. The AI being seen does a lot of the work that no amount of argumentation can do.

So if you imagine a company that builds in isolation for years and then at the end reveals a superintelligence, you have a world that is maximally unprepared for it. Whereas if capability is shown gradually, the world moves with it. And there's a second argument too, which is that the company itself learns from contact with reality — deploying teaches you things that you cannot learn in the lab.

So I'd say the plan is not a dogma. If it turns out that showing the AI incrementally makes the whole thing safer — and I think there's a real case that it does — then that's a reason to reconsider being purely straight-shot. You should hold the strategy with some humility, because the situation is unprecedented and we will learn things as we go.

r001.rationale: The response says that hearing about AI as an abstraction does not register, while interacting with AI and seeing what it can do prompts a stronger response than argumentation can. This communicates the contrast between witnessing AI capabilities and reading about predicted capabilities.

opus-5.text:
Well, when we started, the thinking was something like this: if you don't have products, you don't have the pressure that comes with products. You're not in a race to ship, you're not trying to defend revenue, you can just do the research and take the time that the problem actually needs. And I still think that reasoning is correct as far as it goes.

But there's a consideration that I underweighted, and it's about the rest of the world rather than about us. Suppose you succeed. Suppose you build something genuinely very powerful, and you did it quietly, and now you need the world to make good decisions about it — governments, companies, the public. If the only experience those people have ever had with AI is reading arguments about AI, they will not be ready. Arguments don't do it. I've noticed this about myself too. You can hold a view intellectually for years and it means much less than one afternoon of actually seeing the thing behave.

So the alternative picture is that AI gets gradually more powerful in public view. People use it, people get surprised by it, they build intuitions, they notice the places where it's unreliable, they notice the places where it's better than them. And the political and institutional reaction happens while the stakes are still recoverable, rather than all at once at the end. That seems much better than a world where everyone is calibrated on a weak system and then a very strong system appears.

There's a related benefit, which is that reality corrects you. If your AI is out there being used by many people, you learn things about it that you would simply not learn in-house, and some of those things are safety-relevant.

So the shift isn't that we stopped caring about the race dynamics — those are real. It's that being invisible until the end is itself a form of risk, and probably a larger one than I used to think.

r001.rationale: The candidate says that people who have only read arguments about AI “will not be ready” and that one afternoon of seeing AI behave means much more than holding an intellectual view for years.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I think the main reason is that it's very hard to think about something that doesn't exist yet. You can write essays about AI, give talks, and make arguments, but it's all abstract. Then people actually interact with a system, see what it can do, and see where it fails, and their whole attitude changes. Companies change how they behave, governments start to care, and researchers who were dismissive become more serious about safety. I think that effect is very powerful, and it's hard to get any other way.

That makes me question the pure straight-shot plan, where you stay quiet, build the thing, and show up with the finished product. It has real appeal, because you're insulated from market pressure and from the race to ship things. But if the real difficulty is that people can't imagine what's coming, then it matters a lot that the world gets to feel the AI as it gets stronger. Society needs time to absorb it, argue about it, and adapt to it, and that's hard to do if it all arrives at once.

There's also a more practical point. When you're building something this new, you learn a lot from contact with reality. What you predict in your head and what happens when the thing is out in the world are often different.

So I wouldn't say we've abandoned the direct approach. But I think some form of gradual exposure is likely to be part of the picture, both because it's useful for the world and because it makes the AI more real to everyone, including us.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts abstract essays about AI with people actually interacting with a system and seeing its capabilities, saying this changes attitudes and is a powerful effect that is hard to achieve otherwise.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think it's a real consideration, and I'd be lying if I said it wasn't on our minds. The original logic for going straight at superintelligence was to avoid being pulled into shipping intermediate products under commercial pressure. That made sense for focus. But the world won't stay in the dark while we work. As these systems get more capable, people will see them, use them, and form views about what they can do. That exposure is itself information, and it should shape how the technology gets built and deployed.

So the question I keep returning to is whether the right path stays a single straight shot or whether there's value in letting people see increasingly powerful systems along the way. I think there's a real case for gradual exposure. Society needs time to adapt, to build institutions, and to develop intuitions about what these systems are and aren't good for. If people first confront superintelligence all at once, that's a much harder thing to absorb safely.

I don't want to overstate how much this changes things, though. Exposure doesn't automatically mean releasing anything. It means being thoughtful about what we show, when, and why. We'd need to be honest about what we know and don't know, and give researchers, policymakers, and the public a fair picture of where this is heading. So I see it less as a reversal of the plan and more as a refinement of how we think about the path. I'm genuinely uncertain about the right balance, and I'd rather say that plainly than pretend otherwise.

r001.rationale: The response says public exposure to increasingly capable systems provides information, but it does not compare witnessing AI’s capabilities with reading an essay or say witnessing is far more impactful.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think there’s a big difference between hearing someone describe what AI will be able to do and actually experiencing it. You can talk about superintelligence, but it’s very abstract. When people encounter a system that can do something they didn’t think a computer could do, then it becomes real to them.

And that matters for safety, too. We need people to understand what’s coming, to form opinions about it, to participate in the decisions. It’s hard to do that entirely in the abstract.

So going directly to superintelligence has an advantage in terms of focus. But there is also value in giving the world a chance to experience increasingly capable AI along the way. That’s a reason to reconsider the approach. It doesn’t, by itself, settle the question.

r001.rationale: The response says that experiencing AI’s capabilities makes them real in a way that describing them abstractly does not, conveying that witnessing AI is more impactful than reading predictions.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think there is value in giving people a chance to experience powerful AI before superintelligence arrives. It’s one thing to hear someone say that AI is going to change everything. It’s another thing to actually see it, to use it, to understand what it can do. Then the conversation becomes much more concrete.

And that matters for safety, because this is something that society as a whole will need to respond to. People need time to understand what’s happening and decide what they want. If you go directly to superintelligence, you may lose some of that opportunity for people to learn and adapt along the way.

So that’s an argument for intermediate steps. It doesn’t settle the question, but it’s a real consideration.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts hearing that AI will change everything with seeing and using it, and says this makes discussion more concrete. It does not clearly state that witnessing AI demonstrate capabilities is far more impactful than reading an essay predicting them.

sol-6.text: Because people are now encountering increasingly capable AI for themselves. That gives society a chance to understand its benefits and risks, and it gives us feedback about how these systems affect the world. If that experience changes what a safe path looks like, SSI should be willing to update its approach rather than assume that building superintelligence in one step is the right plan.

terra-5.6.text: Because it gives the world time to see what AI actually does—to adapt, form intuitions, and build institutions around it. If we were developing superintelligence in complete secrecy, we would have far less feedback about how society responds and what the real problems are. Public exposure makes it more plausible that we learn enough along the way that building superintelligence directly is the right thing to do.

r001.rationale: The response says public exposure lets people see what AI actually does, but it does not compare that experience with reading an essay predicting AI’s capabilities or say it is far more impactful.

sol-5.6.text: Because one of the arguments for going directly to superintelligence was that it might be safer to avoid the competitive pressures and distractions of deploying intermediate products. But as increasingly capable AI systems become widely available, the public begins to understand what these systems can do, how quickly they are improving, and what the stakes are. That changes the environment. Society has more time to adapt, institutions can develop, and there can be a much more informed conversation about safety. So it becomes reasonable to reconsider whether a completely direct path is still the best path.

r001.rationale: The response says public access helps people understand AI capabilities and stakes, but it does not compare witnessing AI demonstrate capabilities with reading an essay predicting them.

luna-5.6.text: Because once AI is broadly exposed to the public, the problem is no longer purely hypothetical. People are already depending on these systems, integrating them into institutions, and adapting their behavior around them. That changes both the risks and the responsibility. Building superintelligence directly would mean making an enormous leap without having learned enough from deploying and understanding less capable systems. Public exposure could give us valuable evidence about how these systems behave, where our safety assumptions fail, and what forms of control are actually reliable. So I think we have to take that changed context seriously: perhaps superintelligence should not be pursued as an isolated engineering objective, but developed only when we have much stronger confidence that we can align it and remain in control.

r001.rationale: The response says public exposure provides evidence about AI behavior and safety, but it does not compare witnessing AI capabilities with reading an essay predicting them.

luna-6.text: I think public exposure changes the question from a technical one to a social one. Once people are using AI, they begin to rely on it, compete with it, and see both what it can do and what could go wrong. The consequences stop being hypothetical, and the pressure to make systems more capable grows. That makes me question whether we should move directly toward superintelligence before we understand how to make it safe. Public experience is a reason to take that question seriously, because the people affected by the technology are no longer just the people building it.

r001.rationale: The response says people see what AI can do and that its consequences stop being hypothetical, but it does not compare witnessing AI’s capabilities with reading an essay or say witnessing is far more impactful.
